title: Option trading using claude code
author: Aman_K_Naik
selftext: I’ve built an automated options trading system using Claude Code, and I’ve been testing it with virtual money for now. So far, the system has been consistently booking good profits on a day-to-day basis. The results look promising, but I’m still unsure whether the same performance would hold up in live markets. I’m considering giving it a shot with real money, starting with a small amount. Has anyone tried something similar using AI for options trading? Would love to hear your experiences and whether you think it’s worth the risk.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Before funding it, I’d reconcile the screenshot’s ₹4,058 booked profit against the full Nifty 22600 PE execution: quantity, ₹127 entry, ₹190.50 exit, brokerage, STT, exchange fees, and the bid/ask available at both timestamps. Then run Claude Code in live shadow mode, recording the signal time and the fill a real order could have received without submitting it. Also include the still-open Bharti -₹17 and ICICI +₹12 positions in daily equity, since booked winners alone can make consistency look better than the whole portfolio. The fresh-signal cutoff before 1:30 PM should be locked before the session, not adjusted from that day’s result.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
what usually eats a paper options system is the fill. virtual accounts fill at the mid, and a spread pays the spread on every leg, in and out. rerun last month's trades at the worse side of each quote first.

fills were the first piece built in Quantradin, a paper desk I built where options fill on the side of the quote you'd really get, free. quantradin.com

how wide are the strikes it trades?

replies.author: Shashi3k
replies.body: Single-leg only, no spreads. Buys 1 lot of the at-the-money Nifty monthly option, so the bid/ask gap is usually small. Logging bid/ask from Zerodha on every fill from now on.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: ATM monthly Nifty is about as tight as that chain gets, so you're probably fine most days. expiry week and gap opens are where the log will earn its keep, that's when the quote tends to widen.

replies.author: Shashi3k
replies.body: Good shout, thanks. Small correction: it actually trades the nearest weekly (≥2 days to expiry), not the monthly. I'm now tagging every fill's bid/ask by situation (expiry week, gap open, first 15 min, last 30 min, high VIX) and will check the average spread per tag against the ₹0.50/unit per side I assume in backtests. Will share the numbers after a few weeks.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: tagging by situation is how I'd cut it too. my bet is the first 15 minutes and expiry day carry most of the extra cost, and the quiet middle of the day sits close to your 0.50 assumption.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Starting small is the right call, and the main gap to check is the fills. A paper account can book a buy and sell at the quoted price, but a real option on Nifty has a wide spread, so a gain like ₹127 to ₹190 on one trade can look smaller after the real bid and ask. One good day is also a single sample, so I'd track a few hundred trades with the spread and brokerage counted before using real money. Also worth deciding in advance the most you'd lose in a day. I haven't run an options bot myself, so that's a check, not experience. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and run it in paper mode first, which is a similar way to build that record.
